summary: A status report on FTP implementations and further comments. It lists which hosts have working server and user FTPs, notes that most TENEX servers are nearly identical, and mentions that MIT-Multics has a server that does not listen on socket 3.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo reports which hosts had working FTP programs and proposes clarifications to the protocol. The suggestions cover commands, replies, file transfers and file names.

subtitle: A 1972 FTP status report with proposals for clearer commands and replies.

tldr.problem: Many hosts had working FTP programs, but the protocol documents left some behaviors unclear or awkward.
tldr.mechanism: The memo reports implementation status and proposes changes to command behavior, replies, file names, transfer modes and error handling.
tldr.outcome: The author planned to combine RFC 354, RFC 385 and this memo into a single official FTP document after receiving comments.

sections.title: FTP Implementations and User Features
sections.content:
The author lists hosts with functioning FTP servers and users, and notes that MIT-Multics had both although its server did not listen on socket 3. UCSB was expected to have user and server FTP soon.

The memo describes useful user-program features, including sending messages, transferring files, listing users and directories, and entering commands directly for a server. It notes that file transfer between PDP-10 systems in Image 36 was more efficient than in ASCII 8.
sections.plainLanguage: The report names hosts that had working FTP programs. It also gives examples of extra features added to user programs.

sections.title: An Open-Ended Protocol
sections.content:
The suggestions concern FTP as described in RFC 354 and RFC 385. The author planned to combine those documents and this memo into a single ARPANET Official File Transfer Protocol after comments.

The memo describes FTP as open to experimentation. Sites that agree may define commands, reply codes, data representations, file structures or transfer modes, but additions should be documented clearly enough for other sites to use.
sections.plainLanguage: The author expects FTP to develop. Sites may agree on extra features, but they should explain those features clearly.

sections.title: Commands and Replies
sections.content:
The memo says FTP assumes line-at-a-time interaction with local echo. A server need not provide remote echo and may ignore Telnet control characters, but should not return an error just for receiving them. A Telnet SYNCH should make the server clear the current command line and wait for input such as ABOR.

For multi-line STAT output, the memo proposes a 200 status complete reply to mark the end. It proposes HELP for server guidance, NLST to send file names without other listing details, and reply codes 331 and 433 for account requests. It also describes how STAT and LIST output should be returned.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposals make long replies easier to recognize and add commands for help and file names. They also define replies for cases where an account is needed.

sections.title: Other Protocol Suggestions
sections.content:
The remaining proposals cover accepting default TYPE, BYTE, MODE and STRU settings; allowing multiple recipients for MAIL and MLFL; and choosing a pathname syntax that can work across systems.

The memo also discusses making the final record explicit, extending Telnet SYNCH to more commands, and adding Block mode descriptor codes for a possible error-detection scheme. These are proposals and suggestions, not a claim that every server implements them.
sections.plainLanguage: Other ideas include accepting standard defaults, supporting several mail recipients and making file paths easier to share. The memo also invites comments on possible error checking.
